name: Mobius syndrome
aliases: congenital facial diplegia with abducens palsy

reference.source: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
clinicalPearls: A congenital, non-progressive disorder defined by bilateral (often asymmetric) facial (VII) and abducens (VI) nerve palsies, producing a characteristic mask-like, expressionless face with impaired horizontal gaze and abduction
Presents in the neonate with poor feeding, incomplete eye closure (lagophthalmos), inability to smile and lack of facial expression; drooling and poor lip seal are common
Additional cranial nerve involvement is frequent, especially hypoglossal (XII) causing tongue hypoplasia or fasciculation, and lower bulbar nerves (IX, X) producing dysphagia and aspiration risk

Orofacial and limb anomalies co-occur, including micrognathia, high-arched or cleft palate, talipes equinovarus and terminal transverse limb reduction, with overlap of Poland anomaly and arthrogryposis
Esotropia is common and the horizontal gaze palsy means the eyes cannot abduct past the midline, although convergence and vertical movements are relatively spared
Lagophthalmos with a variably protective Bell's phenomenon places the cornea at risk of exposure keratopathy, so ocular surface lubrication is essential
Now classified within the congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders, reflecting maldevelopment or agenesis of brainstem motor nuclei rather than a primary muscle disease
Cognition is usually normal, but a subset show neurodevelopmental problems including autism spectrum features
reference.pathophysiology: Mobius syndrome is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder resulting from maldevelopment or hypoplasia of the sixth and seventh cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem, with variable involvement of adjacent nuclei (notably XII, IX and X). Both disruptive/vascular and genetic mechanisms are implicated: proposed hypoxic-ischaemic interruption of the developing rhombencephalic vascular supply (associated with misoprostol exposure and, historically, chorionic villus sampling) and, less commonly, defined genetic causes. The end result is absent or deficient innervation of the muscles of facial expression and the lateral recti, on a background of rhombencephalic maldevelopment. Most cases are sporadic.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles and other congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders
Neonatal (transient) myasthenia and congenital myasthenic syndromes
Congenital myotonic dystrophy and other congenital myopathies
Hereditary congenital facial paresis without an abduction deficit
CHARGE syndrome and other syndromic cranial neuropathies
additionalInvestigations: Thin-section brain MRI to assess the brainstem, cranial nerve nuclei and cerebellum
Orthoptic assessment of ocular alignment, ductions and horizontal gaze
Corneal and ocular surface examination for exposure keratopathy
Feeding and swallowing evaluation, including videofluoroscopy, for aspiration risk
Genetic evaluation and counselling, with chromosomal or exome testing if syndromic
Polysomnography if central hypoventilation or sleep-disordered breathing is suspected
redFlags: Aspiration and recurrent chest infections from bulbar dysfunction
Central apnoea or hypoventilation and failure to thrive in the neonatal period
Severe feeding difficulty with poor weight gain
reference.prognosis: The disorder is non-progressive and life expectancy is usually normal once feeding and airway issues are managed, with many patients functioning well given multidisciplinary support. Facial diplegia is permanent, but smile-reanimation surgery (such as gracilis free-muscle transfer) and strabismus surgery can improve function and appearance.
pitfalls: Attributing the expressionless face to intellectual disability rather than to facial palsy
Missing corneal exposure because an intact Bell's phenomenon masks the lagophthalmos
Overlooking aspiration risk and airway compromise in the neonate
Assuming a purely muscular problem and forgetting the brainstem dysinnervation basis
Failing to screen for associated limb, orofacial and neurodevelopmental anomalies
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Protect the cornea from exposure keratopathy with intensive ocular surface lubrication and, where needed, eyelid surgery
Secure feeding and airway safety with modified feeding and formal swallowing assessment, using nasogastric or gastrostomy support and addressing aspiration risk
Correct esotropia and improve ocular alignment with strabismus surgery
Restore a voluntary smile and oral competence with facial reanimation surgery such as gracilis free-muscle transfer
Provide speech and language therapy and orthodontic or craniofacial care for palatal and jaw anomalies
Manage associated limb anomalies such as talipes and reduction defects orthopaedically
Follow up through a multidisciplinary team with audiology, neurodevelopmental support and genetic counselling
